disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.
status.urgent_message: Your HbA1c is 10% or higher. Please contact a doctor soon — within the next few days — rather than waiting for a routine appointment. Seek urgent care if you have extreme thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, confusion or vomiting.

summary: Because your HbA1c is quite high, it's important to contact a doctor soon to discuss these results. Your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, and your main risk factors include low physical activity, being over 45, and having an existing thyroid condition. The most valuable next steps are prioritizing the highlighted tests—especially another HbA1c check, vitamin B12 levels, a dilated eye exam, and a cardiovascular risk assessment—along with building in regular gentle movement and following your calorie target of 1250 and the food guidance provided. Taking these steps soon can help you get a clearer picture of your health and start building healthier daily habits.

comorbidity_assessment.note: Thyroid hormones help regulate metabolism and can influence how your body manages blood sugar and weight. Keeping thyroid function monitored is useful because imbalances can make glucose control and energy levels harder to predict.

constraints: Do not take iodine or kelp supplements unless prescribed.

foods_to_eat: Leafy greens like spinach and kale
Whole grains such as oats, quinoa and whole wheat bread
Legumes including lentils, chickpeas and beans
Non-starchy vegetables like broccoli, zucchini and peppers
Nuts and seeds such as almonds, walnuts and chia seeds
Low-fat dairy like plain yogurt and milk
Olive oil as the main cooking fat
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks like soda and sweetened juices
Refined flour products such as white bread and pastries
Deep-fried foods like chips and fried snacks
Sweets and desserts with added sugar
Processed meats and high-sodium packaged foods
White rice and other refined grains in large amounts
plan.portion_guidance: Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with whole grains like quinoa or oats, and one quarter with a protein source such as lentils, beans or tofu. Use small bowls and katoris to help manage portions, and eat slowly to recognise fullness.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 cups of water through the day. Herbal teas are fine, but limit coffee to one or two cups and avoid sugary drinks.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus
thyroid disorder: no iodine or kelp supplements unless prescribed

exercise: Start with short sessions of gentle activity, such as 10-minute walks, and gradually build up as your energy allows.
Aim to build toward 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, such as walking, swimming, or cycling, spread across most days.
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities (like light resistance bands or bodyweight exercises) on 2 days a week, as energy levels permit.
Because thyroid conditions can affect your energy, listen to your body and adjust pace or duration on lower-energy days rather than pushing through fatigue.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with a 10-minute walk daily this week, then build up gradually to 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, as your energy and comfort allow.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the normal range, so the focus should be on maintaining your current weight through balanced, regular meals and consistent activity rather than trying to lose weight.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool and dark to support restful sleep.
stress: Try slow, deep breathing exercises for a few minutes each day to help calm your nervous system.
Consider gentle practices like mindfulness, meditation, or light stretching, which can help manage stress without overexerting yourself.
Spending time on enjoyable, low-pressure hobbies or connecting with friends can also help reduce stress.
behaviour_change: Since your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, small steady changes in activity and daily routine can support your overall well-being over time.
Keep track of your energy levels alongside your thyroid condition, and share updates with your healthcare provider so your activity plan can be adjusted as needed.
Consider setting small, achievable weekly goals (like adding 5 minutes to your walk) to build confidence and consistency.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Thyroid function (TSH)
monitoring.why: Thyroid problems affect weight, energy and blood glucose control.
monitoring.frequency: Every 6–12 months, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Schedule the highlighted tests soon, especially HbA1c, vitamin B12, a dilated eye exam, and a cardiovascular risk check.
Aim for small amounts of regular movement throughout the day, adjusting intensity based on your energy levels.
Follow your 1250 calorie target and vegetarian meal guidance consistently.
Avoid iodine or kelp supplements unless specifically prescribed by your doctor.
Keep a simple log of how you feel day to day to share with your doctor, especially energy and appetite changes.
